items.title: Rentrée parlementaire en Guinée : « Le contrôle parlementaire n’est pas dirigé contre le gouvernement, il est exercé au service de l’action du peuple » (Dansa Kourouma)
items.description: Ce lundi 5 octobre 2026, l’Assemblée nationale de la République de Guinée a officiellement procédé à sa rentrée parlementaire au titre de la 10ᵉ législature, placée sous le thème : « Construire la Guinée de 2040 : la 10ᵉ législature au cœur de la souveraineté, de la prospérité et de l’intégrité africaine ». Aux côtés des parlementaires guinéens, plusieurs pays de la sous-région étaient représentés par leurs élus siégeant au sein de leurs Assemblées nationales ou de leurs Conseils nationaux de transition. Parmi les délégations présentes figuraient notamment les vice-présidents des Assemblées nationales du Sénégal, de la Côte d’Ivoire, de la Sierra Leone, du Gabon, du Togo, du Liberia, du Mali et de la Guinée-Bissau. À l’issue des interventions des différentes délégations parlementaires, le président de l’Assemblée nationale de la République de Guinée, Dr Dansa Kourouma, a pris la parole pour prononcer son discours, marquant officiellement l’ouverture de la 10ᵉ législature, première de la Ve République. Au cours de cette allocution, qui a duré une quarantaine de minutes, le président de l’Assemblée nationale a abordé plusieurs sujets relatifs à la vie de la Nation ainsi qu’au rôle de la représentation nationale, à laquelle les Guinéens ont confié, à travers leurs suffrages, la mission de porter leurs aspirations durant les cinq prochaines années. Du haut du perchoir, Dr Dansa Kourouma a réaffirmé la détermination des députés à accomplir leur mission avec responsabilité. Il a notamment insisté sur l’esprit qui guidera leur action en matière de contrôle de l’action gouvernementale. « Le contrôle parlementaire n’est ni une position systématique, ni une compréhension précise. Il n’est pas dirigé contre le gouvernement, il est exercé au service de l’action du peuple. Contrôler, c’est aider l’État à mieux faire. C’est vérifier que les engagements sont tenus, que les ressources publiques sont bien employées et que les politiques produisent les résultats attendus pour la population », a-t-il déclaré devant les membres du gouvernement, fortement mobilisés pour la cérémonie. Selon le président du Parlement guinéen, ce contrôle s’inscrit dans un contexte où l’exigence de bonne gouvernance n’a jamais été aussi forte, tant de la part du peuple de Guinée que des plus hautes autorités de l’État. « Elles viennent des citoyens qui veulent voir le fruit de l’information. Elles viennent aussi, et je tiens à le souligner, du sommet de l’État, au plus beau sommet de l’État. Le Président de la République fait preuve d’une exigence croissante quant à la qualité de la gouvernance publique, à la réédition des comptes et à l’obligation du résultat. Je lui rends hommage pour cette rigueur qu’il place l’intérêt du peuple au-dessus de toute autre considération. L’Assemblée nationale entend être, dans le cadre de cette normative, un partenaire exigeant de cette ambition présidentielle », a-t-il indiqué. Poursuivant son intervention, Dr Dansa Kourouma a invité l’ensemble des élus à s’approprier tous les outils mis à leur disposition afin de garantir un contrôle parlementaire plus efficace. « Honorables députés, nous ferons donc un usage plein et responsable de tous les instruments que la Constitution et notre règlement intérieur mettent à notre disposition. Les questions écrites et orales, les questions d’actualité, les auditions des membres du gouvernement et des responsables d’établissements publics, les missions d’information et, lorsque cela sera nécessaire, les commissions d’enquête parlementaires. Et, le moment venu, l’examen de la loi de finances sera le temps fort de ce contrôle, car c’est dans le budget que se lisent les véritables choix des nations ». Par ailleurs, cette figure majeure de la société civile guinéenne et ancien président du Conseil national de la transition a annoncé la volonté de l’institution d’aller encore plus loin dans sa mission de contrôle. « Nous voulons passer progressivement d’un contrôle de conformité à un contrôle de la performance. Il ne suffit plus de savoir si une dépense a été régulièrement engagée. Il faut savoir ce qu’elle a accompli. C’est précisément le sens de l’examen de la loi de finances. Pour un contrôle politique, le contrôle de la performance. Ce contrôle trouvera un terrain d’application majeur dans le programme Simandou 2040 ». Il convient de retenir qu’en plus des responsables parlementaires venus de plusieurs pays d’Afrique, cette cérémonie a enregistré la présence de hauts responsables de la Présidence de la République, de membres du gouvernement, des maires des 13 communes de Conakry, d’anciens ministres ainsi que des responsables des forces de défense et de sécurité, entre autres. Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Rentrée parlementaire en Guinée : « Le contrôle parlementaire n’est pas dirigé contre le gouvernement, il est exercé au service de l’action du peuple » (Dansa Kourouma) est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Forum Alamein-Afrique : Issoufou Mahamadou plaide pour une Afrique intégrée, financée par ses propres ressources…
items.description: À El Alamein, en Égypte, l’ancien Président de la République du Niger et Champion de la ZLECAf, Issoufou Mahamadou, a renouvelé son plaidoyer pour une Afrique plus intégrée, plus solidaire et capable de financer elle-même sa transformation économique. Après avoir porté le projet du marché continental africain, il met désormais l’accent sur un enjeu décisif : mobiliser davantage l’épargne africaine au service du développement de l’Afrique. Le président Issoufou Mahamadou a pris part, le 3 octobre 2026, à la première édition du Forum Alamein-Afrique, organisée en République arabe d’Égypte, ainsi qu’à la Conférence des chefs d’État et de gouvernement de l’Union africaine consacrée à la Zone de libre-échange continentale africaine (ZLECAf). Cette rencontre de haut niveau a réuni des responsables politiques, des décideurs économiques, des représentants d’institutions africaines et des acteurs du développement autour des grands défis de coopération, d’intégration et de transformation structurelle du continent. Placée sous le signe du dialogue, du partenariat et de l’ambition africaine, cette première édition du Forum Alamein-Afrique a offert un cadre d’échanges sur les mécanismes susceptibles d’accélérer l’intégration économique du continent, de stimuler les investissements, de renforcer les échanges intra-africains et de promouvoir des réponses concertées aux défis communs. La participation d’Issoufou Mahamadou à cet important rendez-vous continental s’inscrit dans la continuité d’un engagement de longue date en faveur de l’intégration africaine, du développement durable et de la souveraineté économique du continent. En sa qualité de Champion de la ZLECAf, l’ancien Président nigérien a largement contribué à faire avancer l’ambition d’un marché africain unifié, fondé sur la libre circulation des biens, des services, des capitaux et, à terme, des personnes. Mais l’ouverture des frontières commerciales, ni aussi essentielle soit-elle, ne saurait à elle seule garantir la réussite de cette ambition. Pour devenir une réalité concrète, la ZLECAf doit s’appuyer sur des infrastructures modernes, des corridors de transport performants, une énergie accessible, des réseaux numériques fiables, des capacités industrielles renforcées et des entreprises capables de produire, transformer et commercialiser à l’échelle du continent. Derrière cette ambition se pose une question centrale : avec quels financements construire l’Afrique intégrée de demain ? C’est précisément sur ce terrain que le message porté par le Président Issoufou Mahamadou prend toute sa portée. Après la bataille pour l’intégration commerciale, le défi est désormais de renforcer la capacité de l’Afrique à mobiliser ses propres ressources financières afin de financer ses priorités stratégiques. L’Afrique fait face à des besoins considérables en matière d’infrastructures, d’énergie, d’agriculture, de transport, d’industrialisation, de numérique, de santé, d’éducation et de création d’emplois pour sa jeunesse. Dans le même temps, une part importante de l’épargne institutionnelle africaine notamment celle des fonds de pension, des compagnies d’assurance et d’autres institutions financières demeure investie hors du continent. Ce constat met en évidence un paradoxe majeur : l’Afrique manque souvent de capitaux pour financer sa transformation, alors même qu’elle dispose d’une épargne qui pourrait contribuer davantage à son propre développement. L’enjeu n’est pas de demander aux investisseurs institutionnels africains de prendre des risques inconsidérés. Leur mission première demeure la protection de l’épargne des travailleurs, des assurés et des épargnants. Il s’agit plutôt de créer les conditions permettant à cette épargne de trouver, sur le continent, des projets fiables, rentables, transparents et suffisamment sécurisés. Autrement dit, il ne suffit pas d’appeler l’épargne africaine à revenir vers l’Afrique. Il faut bâtir un environnement économique et financier dans lequel elle aura confiance pour investir durablement. Cela suppose notamment : La préparation de projets bancables dans les infrastructures et les secteurs productifs ; Le renforcement des garanties et des mécanismes de partage des risques ; L’amélioration de la gouvernance économique et financière ; La consolidation des marchés financiers africains ; Le développement d’institutions capables de structurer et d’accompagner les grands projets continentaux ; Le message porté à El Alamein dépasse la seule question du financement. Il renvoie à une vision plus large de la souveraineté africaine. Aujourd’hui, la souveraineté ne se limite plus à la maîtrise du territoire ou à l’indépendance diplomatique. Elle se joue également dans la capacité des États et des institutions africaines à financer leurs infrastructures, à transformer localement leurs ressources, à soutenir leurs entreprises, à développer leur industrie et à créer de la valeur sur le continent. Une Afrique qui exporte principalement des matières premières brutes, importe une grande partie de ses produits finis et dépend largement de financements extérieurs pour construire ses routes, ses chemins de fer, ses centrales électriques et ses industries demeure exposée à une forme de dépendance économique. L’ambition est donc de faire progressivement de l’Afrique un investisseur de sa propre transformation. Les capitaux internationaux conserveront toute leur importance, mais ils devraient venir compléter les capacités africaines, plutôt que s’y substituer. L’Afrique dispose d’atouts majeurs : des ressources naturelles considérables, une population jeune, un marché continental en expansion, des compétences croissantes, une diaspora dynamique et un potentiel important d’épargne institutionnelle. Le défi consiste à relier ces ressources à des projets structurants capables de produire de la croissance, des emplois et une prospérité durable. Tout au long de son parcours à la tête du Niger et dans ses différentes responsabilités africaines et internationales, Issoufou Mahamadou a défendu une vision fondée sur la paix, la stabilité, l’interconnexion des économies, le développement durable et la coopération entre les peuples africains. Alamein-Afrique rappelle la nécessité d’un leadership africain capable de fédérer les énergies autour d’objectifs communs : renforcer la paix et la sécurité, accélérer l’intégration économique, développer les infrastructures, soutenir l’investissement productif et améliorer durablement les conditions de vie des populations. Hier, le combat consistait à convaincre l’Afrique de commercer davantage avec elle-même à travers la ZLECAf. Aujourd’hui, il s’agit également de l’encourager à investir davantage en elle-même. Car le marché continental africain ne pourra déployer tout son potentiel que si les entreprises, les industries, les infrastructures et les chaînes de valeur qui doivent le faire vivre disposent de financements adaptés et durables. À travers le Forum Alamein-Afrique, le continent réaffirme ainsi une ambition claire : transformer ses immenses potentialités en opportunités concrètes, bâtir une économie plus intégrée et plus compétitive, et faire de l’argent de l’Afrique un levier majeur pour l’avenir de l’Afrique. items.title: AIT President Prof Clement Dzidonu urges lifelong learning as AI reshapes work and education
items.description: The President of the Accra Institute of Technology (AIT), Professor Clement K. Dzidonu, has called for a fundamental shift in how individuals, educational institutions, and society approach learning in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). He says graduation should no longer be viewed as the end of a person’s learning journey but as the beginning of a continuous process of developing new skills and capabilities. Professor Dzidonu is advocating what he calls the Sovereign Lifelong Learner, or “Sovereign Triple-L” — an individual who takes personal responsibility for continually renewing, deepening and extending their capabilities throughout their professional and personal life. He argues that the traditional model in which people complete formal education, graduate, enter a profession and rely for years on knowledge acquired at university is becoming increasingly unsustainable. “You went to university. You acquired knowledge. You graduated. You entered a profession. And for many years, much of what you had learned remained relevant to what you were called upon to do. That world is disappearing,” he said. According to Professor Dzidonu, AI, emerging technologies, changing professional practices and the reinvention of industries are rapidly transforming both the nature of work and the capabilities required to remain relevant. He said while university qualifications remain important as recognition of what an individual has achieved at a particular point, they cannot guarantee that the knowledge and capabilities acquired will remain sufficient throughout a person’s career. “The Sovereign Triple-L is not simply someone who keeps taking courses, accumulates certificates, or waits until an employer sends them for training. The Sovereign Triple-L is a Sovereign Lifelong Learner — a person who takes ownership of continuing learning,” he stated. Professor Dzidonu said individuals must increasingly ask themselves what they know, what they can do, what they need to learn and what they may need to unlearn or relearn. He described an individual’s Skills, Expertise, Experience, Knowledge and Know-how collectively as SEEK. He said the rapid pace of technological change is creating what he calls the SEEK-Gap — the changing distance between the capabilities individuals currently possess and those increasingly required to remain effective and relevant. This, he argued, creates a paradox: “The More You Know, the Less You Know.” Professor Dzidonu explained that the concept does not suggest that learning reduces knowledge. Rather, the frontier of what professionals can know and are expected to do continues to expand as AI, new technologies, professional practices and emerging challenges create new demands. He therefore urged individuals to focus not only on accumulating knowledge but on transforming their evolving SEEK into professional capabilities that enable them to solve problems, exercise judgement, adapt, innovate, collaborate and create value. “The future will increasingly belong to those who remain capable of learning what tomorrow requires,” he said. Professor Dzidonu also urged people not to view AI merely as a threat to the knowledge and skills they already possess. “The more useful question is not merely, ‘Will AI make what I learned obsolete?’ It is: ‘How will I use AI, technology, experience, reflection and continuous learning to keep renewing what I know and what I am capable of doing?’” he said. He stressed that becoming a Sovereign Triple-L does not mean surrendering human judgement to AI. Rather, individuals should learn with AI, question it, challenge it and use it responsibly while strengthening their own capacity to think, create, exercise judgement and adapt. At the centre of his proposition is what he calls the Opportunity-Possibility-Difference (OPD) Perspective. He explained this as three stages: See the Opportunity, by recognising that change and disruption can create opportunities for learning; Explore the Possibility, by identifying new skills and capabilities that can emerge from those opportunities; and Create the Difference, by applying those capabilities to solve problems, create value and contribute to society. Professor Dzidonu said the concept extends beyond university graduates to students, professionals, entrepreneurs, educators, business leaders and institutions seeking to remain relevant in a rapidly changing world. “What made an individual capable yesterday may not necessarily be sufficient tomorrow,” he said. His message, he added, is not one of fear or passive dependence on technology but of continuous learning, capability development and personal growth. “Do not allow graduation to become the end of your learning journey. Let it become the beginning of a new one,” Professor Dzidonu stated.

items.title: FWSC to meet striking teacher unions on Tuesday
items.description: The Fair Wages and Salaries Commission (FWSC) is expected to meet the leadership of the three striking teacher unions on Tuesday, October 6, to negotiate their concerns over conditions of service. The meeting follows renewed calls by Education Minister Haruna Iddrisu for the teachers to call off their nationwide strike and return to the classroom. Speaking at the 2026 Ghana Teacher Prize ceremony on Monday, October 5, Mr Iddrisu said the government was committed to resolving the concerns raised by the unions and restoring normal teaching and learning. “May I renew my call to teachers that today is your day. As you celebrate your day today, be reminded that you’re the architects of your future. A strike action can disrupt that future. You must consider calling off the strike action and restoring normalcy,” he said. Mr Iddrisu said the government, under President John Dramani Mahama and supported by Vice President Professor Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, was prepared to engage the unions to find a resolution to the issues. He said the FWSC had been given a mandate by the Minister of Finance to engage the teacher unions on Tuesday. “The government of President John Dramani Mahama, with the support of Vice President Prof. Jane Naana Opoku-Agyemang, will seek to resolve your issues. I assure them that tomorrow [Tuesday], the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission has the full mandate of the Minister of Finance to engage with you to find an amicable way,” he said. The Education Minister also announced that the 20 per cent deprived-area allowance would be paid after the validation of teachers eligible for the allowance is completed. The development comes amid a nationwide strike by the teacher unions over demands for the payment of outstanding arrears, particularly promotion arrears, as well as concerns relating to their conditions of service. Promotion arrears have remained a longstanding issue in Ghana’s pre-tertiary education sector, with teacher unions repeatedly demanding that government clear outstanding payments owed to their members. The outcome of Tuesday’s engagement is expected to determine the next steps in efforts to resolve the dispute and restore normal academic activities in schools.

items.title: Tinubu meets Defence Minister in Lagos, reviews counter terrorism operations
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi President Bola Tinubu has received the Minister of Defence, General Christopher Gwabin Musa (Rtd), OFR, in a high-level strategic meeting at the Presidential Residence in Lagos. A statement by the Ministry of Defence on Monday said the strategic engagement centred on reviewing the national defence framework, evaluating the progress of ongoing counter-insurgency and anti-banditry operations, and aligning inter-agency security strategies to sustain the peace and security of the nation. Speaking during the visit, President Tinubu expressed satisfaction with the steady progress recorded in securing vulnerable communities across Nigeria and reaffirmed his administration’s unwavering commitment to giving full support to the Ministry of Defence. During the meeting, the Minister of Defence provided a comprehensive briefing on current defence initiatives, frontline operational logistics, and proposed reforms aimed at boosting troop morale, modernising hardware capabilities, and strengthening military infrastructure across all regions. General Musa (rtd) expressed gratitude to the President for his continuous guidance and backing of the nation’s security apparatus, assuring the public that the Ministry of Defence remains resolute in executing its mandate with firm resolve and integrity. The meeting forms part of President Tinubu’s continuous security briefings and policy alignment sessions with key government leaders to ensure swift and decisive action against all security and economic challenges nationwide. items.title: Former Trump press secretary Leavitt joins Fox News
items.description: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, will join Fox News to provide “commentary and analysis,” the conservative TV network announced Monday. She will make her debut on November 1, according to a statement from Fox News Media’s Suzanne Scott touting Leavitt’s “a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape.” Leavitt, who gave birth to her second child in the spring, stepped down in late August to focus on her family, while making clear that she intended to continue promoting the “MAGA” (Make America Great Again) brand of right-wing American politics. “I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure,” Leavitt said. She was already a frequent guest on Fox News in her former role. Trump has yet to appoint a new press secretary. Since Leavitt’s departure, the White House has stopped holding regular press briefings. Since leaving the White House, Leavitt has joined an election fundraising organization: MAGA Inc., a pro-Trump political group. At 28, she was the youngest person ever appointed to the high-profile position of press secretary. A native of New Hampshire in the northeastern United States, whose meteoric rise alongside Trump illustrated the spread of his ideas among Gen Z, she spearheaded an aggressive communications strategy targeting traditional media. She also opened the White House to influencers and content creators aligned with the MAGA ideology. Since her departure, Trump’s hostility toward the press has intensified further. He sought to bar CNN and MS NOW, as well as the news outlet Politico, from the White House. A judge ordered the administration to reverse course. items.title: Hématologie : à Rabat, thérapies cellulaires et greffe en débat
items.description: Les 2 et 3 octobre 2026, la capitale a accueilli la quatrième édition des Journées de l'Association des hématologues du secteur privé. Au programme : nouvelles approches diagnostiques et thérapeutiques des maladies du sang, avec un accent sur les hémopathies malignes et les parcours de soins. Les nouvelles approches diagnostiques et thérapeutiques des maladies du sang ont été au centre de cette rencontre, qui a réuni des médecins, enseignants et chercheurs marocains et internationaux, ainsi que des équipes infirmières et d'autres professionnels de santé. Selon un communiqué de l'Association, le programme a alterné conférences spécialisées, discussions et ateliers pratiques, avec une attention particulière portée aux hémopathies malignes et à l'amélioration des parcours de soins. Les participants ont ainsi pu discuter de l'application des évolutions scientifiques et thérapeutiques à la pratique quotidienne, indique l'Association, qui souligne par ailleurs sa volonté de poursuivre ses actions de formation médicale continue tout au long de l'année, auprès des médecins résidents et des hématologues en exercice, afin de contribuer à l'amélioration de la qualité des soins. La première journée a associé les questions d'accompagnement des patients aux sujets plus spécialisés. La gestion de la douleur, la nutrition, l'activité physique et les soins de support ont figuré au programme, aux côtés du séquençage de nouvelle génération, du traitement des lymphomes et des leucémies aiguës et chroniques, de la greffe de cellules souches hématopoïétiques et des thérapies ciblées. Une présentation a par ailleurs été consacrée aux missions et aux perspectives de l'Agence marocaine du sang et de ses dérivés. L'initiative « Vis mon expérience » a également été présentée, avant la tenue de l'assemblée générale de l'Association en clôture de cette première journée. L'un des temps forts de la deuxième journée a été la présentation et la discussion d'un référentiel national de prise en charge de la leucémie aiguë lymphoblastique. Consacré notamment au diagnostic et au parcours du patient, ce document doit être soumis ultérieurement à l'Agence nationale de l'assurance maladie (ANAM), précise le communiqué. Plusieurs sessions ont également abordé les avancées dans le traitement du myélome multiple, notamment les immunothérapies et les thérapies cellulaires, ainsi que les options de prise en charge des formes en rechute ou réfractaires. Les échanges ont aussi porté sur la maladie de Waldenström et la gestion des infections chez les patients atteints de maladies hématologiques. Les travaux se sont achevés samedi par des ateliers pratiques consacrés à plusieurs pathologies nécessitant une prise en charge spécialisée, dont l'hémoglobinurie paroxystique nocturne, l'anémie et la carence en fer, la drépanocytose, l'anémie hémolytique à agglutinines froides et la leucémie aiguë lymphoblastique. items.title: NPP won’t force candidates to step down – Miracles Aboagye
items.description: The opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) says it will not force any aspirant to withdraw from its parliamentary primaries as the party explores ways to identify candidates capable of winning seats in the 2028 general elections. NPP Director of Communications Dennis Miracles Aboagye said discussions and negotiations with potential aspirants are part of the electoral process and do not amount to forcing anyone to step aside. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story , he said the party would assess the circumstances in each constituency before determining the appropriate approach to selecting its parliamentary candidate. “Nobody is asking anybody anywhere to step down. We are saying that discussions, negotiations, conversations are all parts of democracy and the electoral process,” he said. His comments follow a disclosure by NPP flagbearer Dr Mahamudu Bawumia that the party has begun scouting for potential parliamentary candidates across constituencies ahead of the 2028 general elections. Dr Bawumia said the initiative is intended to identify candidates with the potential to win parliamentary seats, rather than relying solely on the outcome of internal primaries. According to him, some aspirants may have the financial resources to win an NPP parliamentary primary but may not necessarily be capable of winning the subsequent general election. Mr Aboagye explained that while some constituencies may have several capable aspirants who would have to compete through the ballot, others may require consensus-building among potential candidates. “There are some constituencies when you go, you identify about four or five capable people. What it means is that all of four or five of them have the capacity to win the seat. You have to put them into the ballot,” he said. He stressed that there would be no one-size-fits-all approach, with the circumstances and dynamics of each constituency determining how the party proceeds. “Election is not the only option in democracy. Negotiations are part of democracy. Sitting down and agreeing to certain things are all parts of democracy,” he said.

items.title: Hegseth’s One Percent
items.description: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is again focusing his attention on junior officers and noncommissioned officers. In a speech delivered September 30 at the Marine Corps base in Quantico, Virginia, he invoked a verse he has frequently cited, Isaiah 6:8— And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying: Whom shall I send, And who will go for us? Then I said: Here am I; send me. Understandably, in these remarks he does not quote a rather more applicable previous verse: Then said I: Woe is me! For I am undone; Because I am a man of unclean lips. Isaiah volunteered for the solitary and dangerous task of reproaching a corrupt court that confused ritual with faith, filled with those who oppress the widow and the orphan, “grind the face of the poor,” and “declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not.” He was, according to the Talmud, eventually sawed in two by the evil king Manasseh. The eighth-century B.C.E. prophet was not joining a military of well more than 1 million men and women with competitive pay, excellent lifelong benefits, and the right to board an airplane ahead of an 80-year-old grandmother. Hegseth is a ludicrous figure in many ways—the strutting sycophant who has promised a military with “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos”; the flaunter of push-ups that are performative but out of regs; the grown man stuck at the development level of an angry first lieutenant; the testosterone-obsessed infantry officer who, unlike most of his peers, never managed to earn a Ranger tab. Even so, we should take what he is saying seriously. [ Read: Pete Hegseth, idea guy ] Following the Quantico speech, Hegseth spoke to cadets at the U.S. Air Force Academy before the annual Air Force–Navy football game. In what is now his stump speech, he called them “the real one percent” of our society who have “a perspective that 99 percent of Americans do not have.” For 251 years, he said, America has required “the absolute best” to stand up and redeem the rest of us. It is not only balderdash, but dangerous balderdash. With the greatest possible respect for the work of the all-volunteer military of the past 50 years—with acknowledgment of its hardship, suffering, and loss—the fact is that the armed forces of the United States have fought the country’s most important and difficult wars not with the one percent, but with all the rest of us: the doughboys and the GIs who cheerfully or reluctantly went when called, and who yearned to get the job done, go home, and resume civilian life. George Washington’s Continentals were vital to winning American independence—but so, too, were the thousands of militiamen who harried British troops. The Civil War was won with mass armies; the American Expeditionary Force of World War I was filled by soldiers inducted through the Selective Service System, as were the armies of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam. In American history, only our lesser wars were fought exclusively with volunteers, and many of those who fought them were recent immigrants looked down upon by those who got here before them. In the fall of 1863, Abraham Lincoln contemplated conscription for the Union armies. In his cool appraisal , he noted: At the beginning of the war, and ever since, a variety of motives pressing, some in one direction and some in the other, would be presented to the mind of each man physically fit for a soldier, upon the combined effect of which motives, he would, or would not, voluntarily enter the service. Among these motives would be patriotism, political bias, ambition, personal courage, love of adventure, want of employment, and convenience, or the opposites of some of these. Just so. People enlist for all kinds of reasons, but not necessarily because they are morally, physically, or mentally the best. Moreover, the brute fact is that the challenges faced by our professional forces have been different from and smaller than those confronted by America’s previous mass militaries of short-term volunteers and conscripts. Again, with respect and gratitude to today’s American soldiers, the Iraqis, Taliban, and Iranians were lesser opponents than the Wehrmacht, the Korean People’s Army, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army, and the People’s Army of Vietnam. Against its more recent enemies, the United States has brought to bear infinitely superior weapons, an array of allies, and usually greater numbers. It is a far cry from American sailors up against Japanese heavy cruisers and German U-boats; American soldiers staring down the barrel of the 88-millimeter gun on a King Tiger tank from a much-flimsier Sherman or watching bazooka rounds bounce off a T-34; or airmen jousting with Russian-piloted MiG-15s over the Yalu River. [ Read: Pete Hegseth’s magic marker ] What is even worse than biblical illiteracy and historical ignorance from this product of Princeton and Harvard Universities is a project about which he seems to be deadly serious: the cultural isolation of the military. His speeches subtly denigrate the general officer corps and focus on the most impressionable segment of the military, those old enough to have bought into the system but young enough to be naive about its merits. What Hegseth is saying amounts to this: Y ou are better than 99 percent of your fellow Americans. You are better physically and morally. You are crusaders, and they—particularly the media and the intellectuals—are not only uncomprehending of your merits but ready to subvert you. They are traitors. We want to select you from a specific slice of society: We want socially conservative young men and (very few) women from Liberty University and Hillsdale, not from liberal research universities and colleges. We want you to be isolated on bases from the rest of this corrupt society, which we despise, as should you. It is profoundly dangerous stuff, the antithesis of what soldiers such as George C. Marshall or Dwight Eisenhower believed, that the soldier is a citizen first, that one cannot adequately defend this society without believing in its values and its essential goodness, that an air of contempt is incompatible with a life of self-abnegation. A Hegsethian cult of military superiority over civilians is not only unwarranted, but actively dangerous. If allowed to fester, it will breed a military detached from America, poorly educated, and contemptuous of the press and all politicians save those of the Trumpian stripe. The force will be narrowly recruited, unrepresentative of a magnificently diverse country, insular, and obsessed with technical matters. It will resemble nothing so much as the Imperial German Army that led its country to disaster in World War I. That the secretary of defense, himself bearing a Crusader tattoo, begins this project by quoting a lonely man of faith is little short of blasphemy.

items.title: Black Stars: Building in the sinking sands
items.description: It is tempting to feel bad for the five-member committee tasked with finding Ghana’s next coach. After all, they have not done anything wrong. Nor do they have any questionable past that should justify the dismissiveness. Take, for instance, Stephen Appiah. Possibly the greatest captain Ghana has ever produced. He is Ghana’s “Mr. Do no wrong” and for good reason. Appiah was captain of a golden generation that delivered Ghana’s first World Cup qualification. Beyond captaining the Black Stars at two World Cups, Appiah has also served as Team Manager and vice chair of the Black Stars Management Committee. Appiah understands the team culture better than most and would know the kind of character required to coach this team. Then there is another former player: Tony Baffoe. Baffoe was once Deputy General Secretary at CAF from November 2017 to June 2021. Since then, he has been preoccupied with running the Professional Footballers Association of Ghana. Fred Pappoe needs no introduction either. In an administrative career spanning decades, Pappoe has served in various roles at the GFA, including as Vice President. The youngest and perhaps the most exciting name is Faisal Chibsah. Faisal Chibsah, brother of former player Yusif Alhasan Chibsah, is a High Performance Specialist He first gained the country’s attention when he was disqualified from the contest for the Technical Director role at the GFA for the crime of being “too young.” Since then, Faisal has taken his young but smart, innovative self to small and ignorant entities like FIFA, which handed him the role of High Performance Expert. Agbesi Dzakpasu is also no stranger to the GFA. He has served as the GFA’s prosecutor and a member of the Legal and Appeals Committees. So, in fairness, the committee has a good mix of experienced administrators, institutional knowledge, understanding of Black Stars culture, and, I dare say, in Chibsah, someone not compromised by association with the old, dysfunctional culture that has led us here. More to the point, whoever they appoint, if they are actually good at what they do and are the right fit for the profile of squad Ghana currently has, should be able to get results. At least some short-term success. But the brutal truth is that this is not just about the competence of the committee and its members. It is simply about the environment, the product of which their decision will be working in, and the conveyor belt that feeds the Black Stars. There are hardly any coincidences in life, and the simultaneous malaise of Ghana’s national teams reflects that more than anything else. There is a direct relationship between the fortunes of the Black Starlets (U-17) , Black Satellites (U-20), and the Black Stars. Ghana’s golden era of 2005 to 2017 was founded on strong youth teams. Derek Boateng (left), Addoquaye Pappoe (middle), and Sulley Muntari celebrate one of Ghana’s goals at the U-20 World Cup in Argentina When Ghana finished as runners-up at the 2001 World Youth Championships in Argentina, the Black Stars benefited. John Paintsil, Addoquaye Pappoe, John Mensah, Michael Essien, Derek Boateng, and Sulley Muntari would later form the nucleus (the others being Stephen Appiah and Laryea Kingston) of the team that qualified Ghana for its first senior World Cup in 2006. Six years later, another Under-20 success, this time as tournament winners in Egypt, would seal Ghana’s return as a proper heavyweight on the continent. Samuel Inkoom, Daniel Opare, Jonathan Mensah, Agyemang Badu, Rabiu Mohammed, Andre Ayew, Dominic Adiyiah and Rabiu Mohammed were instant hits for Ghana. That is how, even with injury depriving Ghana of Essien, Appiah, Laryea Kingston, and Sulley Muntari, Ghana still qualified for a first AFCON final in eighteen years, qualified for the World Cup for a second consecutive time, and were a spot kick from making the semi-final of the World Cup. Three years later, another Under-20 team, while not as successful, produced Baba Rahman, Ebenezer Ofori, Frank Acheampong, and Richmond Boakye Yiadom, who have had varying degrees of successful international careers. Baba Rahman represented Ghana at the youth level In those three Under-20 cycles from 2001 to 20013, Ghana were world champions in 2009, runners-up in 2001 and 2013, and African champions in 2009. That directly translated into Black Stars’ successes. Apart from the already stated World Cup exploits, Ghana made the semi-finals of six consecutive AFCON tournaments and finished second twice. Since then, the only successful spell for Ghana at any level was the U-20 AFCON success in 2021. Ghana has failed to qualify for major tournaments, not just at U-20 level, but at U-17 and even U-23 levels. In total, Ghana has failed to qualify for eight men’s (mostly youth) tournaments. 2020 Olympics 2023 U-17 AFCON 2023 U-20 AFCON 2023 U-20 World Cup 2024 Olympics Men’s Football 2025 U-17 AFCON 2025 U-20 World Cup 2025 AFCON 2025 CHAN The conveyor belt has stopped, and the national team has consequently grieved. Ghana has since suffered a round-of-16 exit at AFCON 2019, consecutive group-stage exits at AFCON 2021 and AFCON 23, while failing to qualify for the last tournament. Curiously, the same allegations of interference in player selections at youth levels exist at senior level, too. Forget that for a moment and look at the coaching turnover. Since assuming office, Kurt Okraku’s administration has hired four coaches for the Black Satellites. That means each coach gets less than two years on the job before they get sacked. The situation is significantly worse with the Black Starlets, where nine coaches have been hired and fired in seven years. It is eerily similar to the Black Stars; seven coaches in seven years. Poor coaching appointments. Poor squad selections, resulting in poor teams. The result is that the best players only play for Ghana when they are already at the senior level, with no prior experience of playing together in a national team, and are completely alien to the team culture and character required. It is also why Ghana shops around the globe for anyone who can pronounce ‘‘jollof’’ to play for Ghana. So it does not matter who picks the poisoned chalice that is the Black Stars coaching job. If the GFA is not deliberate about a well-thought-through, properly resourced, and credible youth program similar to what served Ghana well, any other measure will be a complete waste of time and resources.

items.title: Otti approves N1bn teachers’ fund, reinstates sacked teachers below 65
items.description: By Steve Oko Abia State Governor Alex Otti has approved a N1 billion appreciation fund for teachers and ordered the immediate reinstatement of disengaged teachers who are below the statutory retirement age of 65 years. The governor also directed the payment of outstanding salaries to teachers affected by verification issues, as well as the 4,075 newly recruited teachers who are yet to receive their wages. Otti gave the directives Monday in Umuahia while addressing teachers at the 2026 World Teachers’ Day celebration, declaring that no teacher below 65 years should remain out of service on account of previous disengagement. The governor said the N1 billion fund would be shared equally among teachers in the state, irrespective of when they joined the teaching service. “I have instructed the Accountant-General of the State to share money equally to all of you. “Whether you joined today or you joined 64 years ago, the total amount that I have — the amount for all of you — is one billion naira,” he said. Otti also directed that all teachers whose salaries had been withheld because of verification challenges should be paid by the end of October. He similarly ordered the payment of the 4,075 newly recruited teachers who have not received their salaries. The Governor directed the Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education to immediately return to service all affected teachers below 65 years. “I want to give instructions from here to the Honourable Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education that anybody who is less than 65, if they have been disengaged, you must return them back. “You don’t require any further approval, I’ve given the approval from here — please bring all of them back, even if it is six months before retirement. Bring them back,” Otti ordered. The governor said the decision was in line with his administration’s commitment to fairness and transparency, stressing that government must be consistent with its pronouncements. On promotion arrears, Otti directed the Abia State Universal Basic Education Board, ASUBEB, to conclude the processing of teachers’ 2021 and 2022 promotions and harmonise the process with the State Head of Service for his approval. He directed that the affected teachers be promoted before the end of October. The governor also ordered the immediate payment of outstanding check-off dues, giving the Accountant-General seven days to clear the arrears. Otti said several of the concerns raised by the Nigeria Union of Teachers had already been addressed, while others were receiving attention. He said his administration’s investment in education was aimed at repositioning the sector as the foundation for the state’s development, stressing that the ongoing development of smart schools across the 17 local government areas was designed to prepare pupils for the future without undermining conventional education. He reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to free and compulsory education, while congratulating Abia pupils who excelled at the international schools debate championship in Qatar and those who topped the National Examinations Council, NECO, examinations. Earlier, the Commissioner for Basic and Secondary Education, Elder Goodluck Ubochi, said the theme of the 2026 World Teachers’ Day celebration, “Standing with Teachers: Protecting the Profession, Advancing Citizens, and Serving Our Teachers,” underscored the strategic role of teachers in nation-building. Ubochi listed teacher recruitment, professional development, improved school infrastructure, modern learning environments and smart schools among the reforms being implemented by the administration. The state Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Teachers, NUT, also acknowledged improvements in the sector, including increased budgetary allocation, mass recruitment, free and compulsory basic education and the extension of teachers’ retirement age from 60 to 65 years. He, however, appealed for further improvement in teachers’ welfare and resolution of outstanding challenges. The celebration featured a march-past by teachers from across the state. The post Otti approves N1bn teachers’ fund, reinstates sacked teachers below 65 appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: L’UE autorise les expulsions des sans-papiers, dont les Algériens, vers des pays tiers
items.description: Bien que controversé, le « Règlement retour », qui prévoit notamment le placement des personnes expulsables dans des hubs de rétention dans des pays tiers, a été adopté par le Conseil de l'Europe. Le nouveau règlement est entré en vigueur vendredi 2 octobre. Les clandestins algériens en Europe sont concernés par les nouvelles dispositions. Le règlement porte sur l’éloignement forcé des étrangers faisant l’objet d’une obligation de quitter le territoire d’un État membre de l’UE. Les défenseurs du texte le présentent comme une solution qui permettra d’éloigner les sans-papiers refusés par leurs pays d'origine, sachant que seules 20 % des expulsions sont actuellement effectivement exécutées. Sans-papiers : des « hubs retour » pourront s’ouvrir partout dans le monde Selon un communiqué de la Commission européenne, le règlement prévoit des sanctions à l’encontre des étrangers qui refusent de quitter le territoire de l'État membre ou qui ne coopèrent pas avec les autorités. Les sanctions possibles sont la réduction des allocations, le refus des aides au retour volontaire, des amendes ou des sanctions pénales si le droit national le prévoit. Les décisions prises par chaque État pourront être reconnues par les autres États membres. La reconnaissance est facultative, mais elle pourra être rendue obligatoire dans trois ans. Le règlement retour prévoit la possibilité de prononcer une interdiction d'entrée à durée indéterminée ou une rétention de plus de 24 mois. Les États membres pourront envoyer des personnes expulsables vers des centres de rétention à l'étranger, à l’exception des mineurs non accompagnés. Les familles avec enfants pourraient être en revanche concernées. Les centres de rétention, ou « hubs retour », pourraient s'ouvrir partout sur la planète dans des pays qui « respectent les normes internationales en matière de droits humains, dont le principe de non-refoulement », précise-t-on. Les recours ne sont plus suspensifs de l’expulsion Les expulsés pourront donc se retrouver dans un pays avec lequel ils n'ont parfois aucun lien. Ils sont placés sur la base d’une évaluation au cas par cas, « s’ils ne coopèrent pas, s’ils présentent un risque de fuite ou s’ils constituent une menace pour la sécurité », précise le Conseil de l’Europe. Les concernés pourront se voir, en outre, interdits d’entrer sur le sol européen pendant 10 ans, voire pour une durée maximale de 20 ans, pour des motifs dûment étayés. L’autre nouveauté, c'est la fin de l’automaticité du caractère suspensif du recours contre la mesure d’éloignement. Ce qui signifie qu’une expulsion peut avoir lieu même si un recours a été introduit. Le règlement donne aussi aux autorités la possibilité de fouiller les personnes et leurs biens, et de « saisir leurs effets personnels et appareils électroniques ». « Chasse aux sorcières » Les détracteurs du texte entrevoient déjà la « chasse aux sorcières » qui ciblera les sans-papiers. « Ce Règlement intensifie la détention des migrants et les expulsions, encourage une chasse aux sorcières contre les personnes sans papiers et donne aux États membres carte blanche pour envoyer des personnes vers des destinations qu’elles ne connaissent même pas », a déploré Chiara Catelli, chargée de plaidoyer à l'ONG belge PICUM, citée par le site Info Migrants. Pour elle, les nouvelles dispositions vont « accroître, et non réduire, la situation irrégulière ». « De plus en plus de personnes auront peur de s’adresser aux services publics ou de demander une protection, par crainte d’être placées en détention ou expulsées », explique-t-elle. L’article L’UE autorise les expulsions des sans-papiers, dont les Algériens, vers des pays tiers est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Court reserves judgment in suit seeking Mark, Aregbesola’s removal
items.description: The Federal High Court in Abuja on Monday reserved judgment in a suit filed by Mr Nafiu-Bala Gombe, seeking to stop the David Mark-led leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) from parading themselves as leaders of the party. Justice Peter Lifu adjourned the judgment to a date that would be communicated to parties in the suit. The judge made the decision after lawyers to the plaintiff and the defence adopted their processes and presented their arguments for and against the case. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Justice Lifu had, on June 16, dismissed the application seeking his recusal from the case. The judge, who held that the two motions filed by ADC and Ogbeni Rauf Aregbesola (1st and 3rd defendants) lacked merit, awarded a fine of N1 million each against ADC and Aregbesola, the embattled National Secretary of the party, in favour of Gombe. ADC and Aregbesola had, in separate motions, asked Justice Lifu to withdraw from the suit filed by Gombe, an aggrieved party member, citing alleged bias. NAN reports that Gombe, in the suit, is seeking an order restraining Mark, Aregbesola and members of their interim National Working Committee (NWC) from parading themselves as the party’s leaders. He had argued that the emergence of Mark, Aregbesola and other interim NWC members as the party’s leaders breached the provisions of the party’s constitution and the Electoral Act. Gombe had sued ADC, Mark, Aregbesola, Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and Ralph Nwosu as 1st to 5th defendants respectively in the suit marked: FHC/ABJ/CS/1819/2025. Nwosu was the former ADC National Chairman who stepped down for the Mark leadership of the party. (NAN) The post Court reserves judgment in suit seeking Mark, Aregbesola’s removal appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Low inflation on paper, high cost of living: How Presidents Mahama and Trump are facing stark economic reality
items.description: A new AP-NORC poll in the United States has become the latest warning sign for governments touting low inflation figures while citizens complain of high cost of living. The poll, released Thursday October 1, 2026, shows 82% of Americans disapprove of President Donald Trump’s handling of cost of living, with only 17% approving, even though US inflation is reported at 3.4%. In Ghana, a similar situation is unfolding under the Mahama administration with Ghanaians complaining about the disconnect between reported low inflation and the cost of living. While inflation on paper is reported at around 5%, Ghanaians say utility tariffs, fuel prices, transportation, rent and prices of goods and services keep rising sharply. The frustration in Ghana is visible across Ghanaian social media, and on the ground, with widespread reactions about rising electricity costs, in particular, and general high costs. Author Chris-Vincent Agyapong in a July Facebook post complained about the high cost of living and doing business in Ghana, comparing printing costs of his book – 7 GHS in China versus 23 GHS in Ghana. In another instance, supermarket shopper Mohammed Hassan Albezem posted a video from a supermarket in Ghana lamenting how the total cost at the till is “getting closer to your salary.” Last week, content creator Ama Morton posted a video on September 28 titled “rent in Accra is not a joke,” detailing exorbitant rent demands in the capital and sparking debate on the housing crisis. On food prices, blogger Ray Michael, in a viral post titled “Ghana is hell”, listed fufu selling at over GH¢300 in East Legon and daily meals costing 150-250 cedis. Commenters under the posts summed up the mood, corroborating the posts with their own experiences of high cost of living, with emphasis on high cost of electricity, transportation and food. Market women count losses In the markets, the pain is even more direct, as traders say produce is rotting because buyers have no money. “We bring tomatoes and pepper and they rot. People come and say they used all their money to pay light bill and water,” a trader at Makola said. “We buy at a high price but when we add small profit, nobody buys. The goods stay and spoil,” a vegetable seller at Kaneshie Market also lamented. “Our plantain rots on the farm and in the market. Transportation is high, rent is high, people are not buying like before,” a trader who brings goods from the Eastern Region said. Both in the US and in Ghana, under the administrations of Presidents Trump and Mahama, the story is the same – despite low inflation on paper, citizens say the cost of living keeps rising, and market women say their products are rotting on farms and in markets as people are not buying. Ironically, both Presidents staged comebacks after they were voted out of office after their respective first terms.

items.title: ‘Abandoned province’: Amir Muqam slams PTI, says not in favour of governor’s rule in KP but security risks persist
items.description: Minister for Kashmir Affairs and Gilgit-Baltistan Amir Muqam on Monday slammed the PTI-led government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, stressing that the federal government was not “in favour of governor’s rule” amid the party’s march, but warning of national security risks. The minister’s comments came as KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi launched the party’s long march towards Islamabad on Sunday, saying that the party would “not accept” any policy against the interests of the people of KP. PTI went ahead with its march despite warnings from the federal government. The government has threatened to send the PTI government in KP packing by imposing governor’s rule or an emergency if the party proceeded with the march. The march was announced as part of its nationwide protest to demand the release of its founder, Imran Khan. It has become a major bone of contention between the government and the main opposition party, with both taking entrenched positions. Addressing a press conference on Monday, Muqam said, “We are not in favour of having governor’s rule or declaring an emergency in KP as politically it is not a good decision; however, on the one hand, you have politicians, and then there is the state. Politics can only continue if we still have control of the province.” He claimed that the provincial government had lost its writ and that “the security situation was deteriorating day by day”. Speaking about the recent negotiations with the opposition over the party’s march to Islamabad, the minister said the government’s side had suggested that they “be on the same page” about terrorism. Muqam said the province’s chief executive had “abandoned” the province. “There is no sign of the government in the province. The chief executive of the province stays busy with his one-point agenda.” He said terrorism was not limited to KP. Muqam went on to warn, “If KP is overtaken by terrorists [..] then the rest of Pakistan would not remain free either.” He said the provincial government, the federal government and the armed forces “should be on the same page” in counterterrorism efforts. Shifting his attention to the weekend’s negotiations with the opposition, Muqam applauded the opposition’s delegation, saying that they were willing to find a resolution. He recalled that during the first day of the talks, the opposition asked for an extension since the KP CM needed to be a part as well. “The next day, we came back and sat from 3pm till 3am. In the talks, three to four drafts were prepared, and at one point, it was decided that we would issue a joint statement.” He said that at the time, the opposition’s delegation had assured the government side of their cooperation. He recalled that the “interference” began after 9pm on Saturday. “Messages came in asking for clauses to be added and removed. In the end, we had a deadlock,” Muqam said. The minister said it was “highly unfortunate” that the talks had ended. He also questioned how the KP CM was making statements regarding the march while “his nominated people were engaging in talks”. He claimed that government-related work in KP had come to a halt over the past two to two-and-a-half months. Muqam reiterated that the federal and provincial governments “needed to be on the same page”. He also questioned the provincial government’s “lack of seriousness” over the National Action Plan (NAP). “Why have you held only one meeting in the entire year? How many martyrs have you visited?” Muqam asked. “In fact, you went against the police to try to rob them of their authority,” he said, referring to the KP Police Act, 2026. During his press conference, Muqam reiterated that PTI’s march would not be allowed to enter Islamabad. “What is this drama of proceeding with the march when you know fully well that you will not be allowed to enter Punjab?” Muqam said to PTI. He questioned whether the KP government had spoken about the rights of the people of KP. “It is the state’s responsibility not to leave the people of KP at the mercy of terrorists, and for that, there is a constitutional way to provide them relief,” the minister said, in an apparent reference to governor’s rule. Asked about further negotiations with the opposition, the minister said the “door to talks is still open […] if it is for the betterment of the country, we are always ready to talk”. ‘Terrorism, not politics, is the problem’ Separately, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif also emphasised the gravity of the security situation in KP and appeared to be holding the PTI’s provincial government responsible for the prevalent terrorism. “The state and KP’s problem is not politics but terrorism,” he began in a post on X before sharing terrorism-related data. According to Asif, around 6,200 terrorism incidents took place in the province over the past two years, 1,200 personnel were martyred and 37 suicide attacks by Afghans were recorded. “Fourteen suicide attacks have taken place in the ongoing year, most of which have the involvement of Afghans.” Moving on to law enforcement agencies, he said the total number of police personnel in KP was 125,000 and 13,000 among them were deployed for VIP protocol. On the other hand, he said, 17,000 police posts remained vacant “in a province where police are playing an important role [against] terrorism”. He went on to allege that the “Counterterrorism Department’s (CTD) system is nearly non-functional in the merged districts”. According to Asif, the department had just 17 bulletproof vehicles and the total number of CTD personnel was around 3,300. Among them, only 25 were permanent employees and rest were contract-based employees, he said. The defence minister then accused the government of trying to undermine the police’s capacity by “using the Police Act 2017 for political purposes”. He further alleged that police had sought funds worth Rs42 billion for the reconstruction of police posts, but the provincial government released just Rs1.2bn. “Lives are being lost every day due to the non-provision of funds. On the other hand, expenditure of Rs42bn has been claimed in papers, when in reality, this amount has been embezzled,” he said. In this scenario, Asif said, the PTI’s stance had been that if security forces had been guarding the frontiers, then how were terrorists able to infiltrate into the country. Noting that the PTI had been in the government in KP for the past 13 years, he alleged that “Imran had a soft spot for the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)” — an outlawed terror outfit — and the PTI’s view had been more inclined towards holding talks with terrorists. He accused Imran of “pushing the entire security system towards talks with the TTP and its allied groups”. “Pakistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa paid the price for this policy,” he regretted. “Yet, this party (PTI) is talking about engaging the TTP and TTA (Tehreek-i-Taliban Afghan) today.” The defence minister asserted that the state had a clear policy on terrorism now. “The state’s policy is to not hold talks with terrorists but to take action against them.” Asif said the KP government’s policy was contrary to the state’s policy. He said there had been accusations that the fight against terrorism was for “dollars”. “Tell us, how many billions of dollars has America provided to Pakistan in the past few years for the fight against terrorism and security?” he questioned. “Tell us, are the drone strikes in Kohat and Peshawar and the TTA attacks on Pakistani security posts not real? When terrorists themselves are using drones, why can’t the army use drones for its own defence?” Raising several questions regarding counterterrorism measures taken by the PTI, he also refuted the KP government’s allegation that they were not being provided funds by the Centre. “There is no lack of funds, but corruption and weak governance diminish their impact,” he claimed. The defence minister went on to say, after claiming funds transfers to KP on several accounts, that “the number of pending prosecution cases is approximately 3,000, but no terrorist has been executed yet, nor has any punishment been awarded”. He said the state’s clear policy was “hold, build and transfer”. “First secure and hold the areas, then begin reconstruction and build an institutional structure and then transfer [the control] to the civil administration,” he elaborated. “The question is why are you not applying the policy of hold, build and transfer in these areas? Your judiciary and civil administration should step forward to take charge of managing these areas,” he concluded. Separately, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said that a return to negotiations was possible if there was an assurance of positive progress by the opposition regarding counter-terrorism efforts in KP. Speaking on Geo News ’ programme “Capital Talk”, he said that the federal government aimed to end terrorism in Pakistan, protect its borders and keep people safe. “The provincial government will have to play its role at any cost in this policy and operation,” he added. He added that both sides were still in contact, and said that if “better sense prevails” amongst the opposition and they could provide “assurance of some positive progress” in this regard, then they could sit down for more talks. Opp-govt dialogue failure Over the weekend, the government and opposition held two rounds of talks , which did not yield positive results, with counterterrorism policies and access to Imran emerging as two major sticking points. On Sunday, the PTI said it wanted immediate access to party chief Imran for consultations, and even agreed to forgo other demands in return for a meeting with Imran. However, the government declined to make access to Imran part of the proposed agreement, the opposition party claimed. Another deadlock was terrorism in KP. The federal government asked the KP government to support its counterterrorism measures and support emergency measures within 72 hours in the merged tribal districts, the PTI said. Instead, the PTI proposed that authorised representatives of the federal and KP governments meet within 72 hours to develop a clear, comprehensive and mutually agreed strategy for peace and counterterrorism, the statement added. The PTI said the health and medical treatment of Imran Khan was also raised as a matter of fundamental importance. Meanwhile, PTI leader Salman Akram Raja, who was a part of the opposition’s delegation, said the primary reason for the failure was disagreement on anti-terrorism actions in KP. Raja said the opposition stood firm on its principled position that anti-terrorism actions should be based on an agreement between the federal government and the KP government, and would be framed in consultation with stakeholders. After talks between the government and the opposition ended without headway, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Sunday accused CM Afridi of “sabotaging” negotiations. On Sunday, Naqvi also held a meeting with the KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi to discuss the political and security situation amid speculations of ‘imminent’ governor’s rule in the province. A government source told Dawn that the government was seriously considering the imposition of the governor’s rule in KP. But, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Monday that a return to negotiations was possible if there was an assurance of positive progress by the opposition regarding counterterrorism efforts in KP. Speaking on Geo News ’ programme ‘Capital Talk’, he said that the federal government aimed to end terrorism in Pakistan, protect its borders and keep people safe. “The provincial government will have to play its role at any cost in this policy and operation,” he added. He said that both sides were still in contact, and said that if “better sense prevails” amongst the opposition and they could provide “assurance of some positive progress” in this regard, then they could sit down for more talks.

items.title: Alleged drug deal: Court invites NDLEA chairman in Abba Kyari’s trial
items.description: The Federal High Court in Abuja has directed the Chairman of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) to produce in court the list of the personnel who were on duty on Jan. 19, 2022 at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu State. Julius Mba, counsel to Abba Kyari and Insp. Simon Agirgba (1st and 3rd defendants), made this known on Monday before Justice Emeka Nwite while seeking an adjournment, following the absence of the defence witness in court. Kyari, the former head of the defunct Police Intelligence Response Team (IRT), alongside four other suspended IRT officers, including the two now convicted drug traffickers, were initially being prosecuted by the NDLEA on an eight-count charge. The agency accused Kyari and the officers of tampering with the cocaine the IRT officers recovered from the arrested drug traffickers at the airport. The four officers are ACP Sunday J. Ubua; ASP Bawa James, Insp. Simon Agirgba and Insp. John Nuhu, named as 2nd to 5th defendants respectively. Although the two convicted drug traffickers, Chibunna Umeibe and Emeka Ezenwanne, listed as 6th and 7th defendants, pleaded guilty to the counts, Kyari and his men pleaded not guilty to the counts against them. When the case was called on Monday, NDLEA lawyer, Joseph Sunday, informed the court that the matter was scheduled for continuation of hearing. He said the prosecution was ready to proceed, subject to the convenience of the court. Responding, Mba said he confirmed that the case was slated for continuation of the evidence of the 2nd defence witness (DW-2), John Nwonke, who is a subpoenaed witness. He, however, said unfortunately, there was a letter filed on behalf of the same witness, informing that he was illed. He said the letter, dated Oct. 2, was addressed to the deputy chief registrar of the court and that the lead defence counsel, Onyechi Ikpeazu, SAN, was also copied. The lawyer told the court Nwonke was illed at the moment and they were only praying that he gets well to continue and conclude his evidence. “On that note, we may not be able to put in a witness today because this is a criminal trial and a very serious one at that matter,” he said. Mba stated further that they had the instruction of Ikpeazu, who was representing Kyari and Agirgba, but unavoidably absent, to equally file a “subpoena duces tecum” to be served on the NDLEA boss. He said the subpoena duces tecum was filed on Sept. 30 and graciously signed by Justice Nwite on Oct. 2. “But we only received this, this morning my lord,” he said. According to him, the subpoena duces tecum is requiring the NDLEA, through the DG, to produce before this court for inspection and use of this honourable court, the certified true copy of all the list of personnel of the agency who were on duty on 19th day of January, 2022, at Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu State for proper consideration and for the defence of 1st and 4th defendants sir. A subpoena duces tecum is a legal court order that commands a person or business to bring specific physical or digital evidence to a legal proceeding. Responding, the NDLEA lawyer said he was just seeing Nwonke’s letter. “We have been here since morning and there is no courtesy at all to show us the letter and tell us the position of the witness. “In any case, we will be opposing the application for adjournment,” Sunday said. The lawyer argued that the his objection was predicated on the fact that the application was in bad taste which was calculated to subvert the administration of criminal practice. He said contrary to Mba’s submission, on the last adjourned date, a lawyer (A.A. Akas) who appeared for Kyari notified the court that the DW-2 (Nwonke) was on official duty outside the country. Sunday recalled that the court, before the adjournment, ordered that Nwonke should “be present in court today so that the case could proceed with the warning that any unseriousness will warrant the foreclosure of the defence.” According to him, interestingly today, Akas Esq. is not present in court and the counsel in court has totally circumvented the specific orders of my lord. Sunday alleged that Mba came up with a letter from a purportedly sick witness. But Mba disagreed with Sunday’s use of words. “My Lord, I cannot stand here and be insulted by my learner brother. “This is not my letter; a letter is not coming from me, and for my learner brother to say I circumvented the order of courr, I take exception to this sir,” Mba said. After the judge’s intervention, Sunday moved an oral application seeking an order foreclosing the evidence of the DW-2. The NDLEA argued that the letter did not disclose the withess’ nature of sickness and the hospital he was receiving treatment. Besides, he said “the DW-2 has turned himself into a medical doctor and taking the position of God to determine that the sickness will be for exactly two weeks.” Sunday submitted that this was not a letter the can could consider. “I don’t think we can base any adjournment on this matter,” he argued. Resoonding to the issue of subpoena, the NDLEA lawyer said none of the prosecution team had been served with the letter. “We don’t conduct trial by ambush. We are not aware of any subpoena my lord,” he said. The lawyer, who urged the Court to order the defence to proceed on their next witness, prayed the court to foreclose Nwonke’s evidence “and treat him as having given a testimony that was not subjected to cross-examination.” But Mba disagreed with Sunday’s argument. He stated that his application was predicated upon fair, just and full determination of their defence on the merit and in the interest of justice, equity and fairness. “It is not a matter of sentiment my lord,” he said. He clarified that the information available to Akas, as at the last adjourned date, was that the witness was on official assignment. “That has not changed,” he said, adding that upon his arrival, he wrote to court that he was indisposed. He also restated that though they had applied for the subpoena lettter some day’s ago, he only received it on Monday after it was signed by the judge on Oct. 2. Delivering the ruling, Justice Nwite held that Nwonke (DW-2)’s letter was not convincing enough for the court to grant the request for an adjournment. The judge, however, held that in the interest of justice, the case would be adjourned until Oct. 7 for the continuation of the witness’ testimony and cross-examination. “Failure of the witness to appear on the said date means that his testimony will be foreclosed,” he ruled. The judge also ordered lawyers to the 1st to 5th defendants to submit to the court the names of the witnesses they intend to call before the next adjourned date. (NAN) The post Alleged drug deal: Court invites NDLEA chairman in Abba Kyari’s trial appeared first on Vanguard News .
